narrative:
After carefully reviewing your application, the admissions system flagged a significant concern about your likelihood of passing the bar exam on the first attempt, estimating a 51% probability of not passing — a margin that, while not overwhelming, was enough to result in a rejection decision. This outcome was shaped by a combination of factors from your academic record and personal circumstances, and understanding them in detail may help you chart a stronger path forward.

The single most influential factor in this decision was your academic performance during your third year of law school, where your class standing placed you in the 1st decile — meaning you ranked in the bottom 10% of your cohort. Among students who successfully passed the bar exam, the average third-year class standing sits around the 6th decile, so this gap is substantial and weighed heavily against your application. Third-year performance is particularly telling because it reflects how well a student has consolidated their legal knowledge heading into the bar exam, and the model treated this as a strong signal of risk.

Importantly, two other factors actually worked in your favor and pushed back against the failure prediction. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.70 is notably higher than the 3.24 average among students who passed the bar, and this was the second most influential factor — pulling the prediction in a positive direction. Similarly, your LSAT score of 34, while slightly below the average of 37.27 among successful students, still contributed modestly toward a more favorable outcome in the model's assessment.

The tension in your profile is clear: your pre-law academic record suggests genuine intellectual capability, but your in-school performance — particularly by your third year — raised serious concerns about bar exam readiness. It's also worth noting that you are enrolled part-time, a circumstance shared by fewer than 7% of students who passed the bar, and your lower-middle family income background may reflect real-world pressures that can make full academic focus more difficult.

Given all of this, the most meaningful step you can take is to address your law school academic performance directly. Consider whether additional bar preparation resources, tutoring, or a change in your study approach could help you demonstrate stronger mastery of the material. If you are able to retake courses or improve your standing before reapplying, that would likely have the greatest impact on a future application outcome.
